html:
The Fang, a Bantu-speaking people, moved south and west through the forests of what are now Cameroon, mainland Equatorial Guinea and Gabon in the 18th and 19th centuries, reaching the coast by the late 1800s.

They came in small clan groups, clearing farms and trading ivory and rubber with European houses on the coast. Their arrival pushed aside or absorbed smaller coastal peoples. European travellers were struck by their ironwork and their carved reliquary guardian figures, later collected in Paris.

Today the Fang make up the large majority in Equatorial Guinea, where both post-independence presidents, Macías Nguema and Obiang, came from Fang clans of the mainland. In Gabon they are the largest single group, and the Bwiti religion took its modern form among them.
sum: The Fang, a Bantu-speaking people, moved south and west through the forests of what are now Cameroon, mainland Equatorial Guinea and Gabon in the 18th and 19th centuries, reaching the coast by the late 1800s.
